solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Book his car company to travel around Spain

indicators.note: around says the reworked letters wrap themselves about another piece
letters that travel move about and end up somewhere else in the order

parts.note: all three words taken as written, thirteen letters of raw material
E is the international vehicle code for Spain (España)

explanation.surface: Someone books a hire car from a company for a trip around Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole phrase his car company is the fodder; the car-hire picture hides that the fourteen-letter answer is a novel title.
explanation.definitionFit: Bret Easton Ellis's 1991 novel about a Manhattan serial killer is a book, so the single word stands for its title.

clue.text: Mr Right that Sebastian Melmoth knocked out?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the perfect man to marry
second meaning: Sebastian Melmoth was the alias Oscar Wilde used in exile, and to knock out is to write quickly, so this is a Wilde comedy

explanation.walkthrough: Knocked out suggests a boxer flattening Mr Right; here it means dashed off, as a writer produces a play. AN IDEAL HUSBAND is Wilde's 1895 comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Right is the colloquial name for the perfect future spouse, and Wilde's play carries exactly that phrase as its title.

clue.text: Donne was one to upset English society and leg it

indicators.note: to upset something is to knock it over and throw its contents into disorder

parts.note: E is the standard abbreviation for English
S is the standard abbreviation for society
the two words run together as written

explanation.surface: John Donne upsets polite English society and has to run away.
explanation.walkthrough: Leg it is British slang for run away, but here the two words just supply letters.
explanation.definitionFit: John Donne wrote elegies, mournful poems for the dead, so he was a writer of that kind of poem.

clue.text: Childish little introduction pulled from Taxi Driver?

indicators.note: pulling the introduction from a word strips away its opening letter

parts.note: Travis Bickle is the cab driver in Scorsese's film Taxi Driver

explanation.surface: A cute, childish little opening scene is cut from the film Taxi Driver.
explanation.walkthrough: Taxi Driver is not a cabbie in general but the film, and its title character's surname loses its B.
explanation.definitionFit: Ickle is a baby-talk form of the word meaning small, used jokingly or in speech to young children.

clue.text: Royal Society plays with short satanic mechanics

indicators.note: someone who plays with things moves them around and rearranges them
short says the word that follows is cut off before its last letter

parts.note: RS is the abbreviation for the Royal Society
taken as written before it is cut

explanation.surface: The learned Royal Society dabbles in devilish experiments with machinery.
explanation.definitionFit: Mechanic is an old word for a manual worker or craftsman, so skilled manual workers are mechanics in that sense.

clue.text: It was broken by Valjean and Monsieur Thénardier in the theatre?

parts.note: the innkeeper Thénardier is Éponine's father, a pa
his stage part is a role in the theatre

explanation.surface: Two characters from Les Misérables, one a convict and one a scoundrel on stage, both break something.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that Thénardier is defined by what he is in the show: a father, and a part to be played.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean Valjean breaks the terms of his conditional release from prison, which is what this word means.

clue.text: Money man's novel response to cuts? He howls!

parts.note: to yell 'ow' is how anyone responds to a cut
a dog is something that howls

explanation.surface: A cash-strapped writer cries out at spending cuts and howls in protest.
explanation.walkthrough: Money is not cash but the 1984 novel by Martin Amis, so the money man is Amis and this is his 2003 novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Martin Amis, author of the novel Money, published Yellow Dog in 2003, so it is a novel by that author.

clue.text: One in Hardy novel heading to imbibe pitchers

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are made into something new

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

indicators.note: the heading of a word is the letter at its top

parts.note: the opening letter of imbibe

explanation.surface: A character in a Thomas Hardy novel takes to drinking from jugs.
explanation.walkthrough: Hardy novel suggests a book title, but novel is the anagram signal working on the surname.
explanation.definitionFit: A hydria was an ancient Greek water jar with three handles; the Greek plural form names several such jugs.

clue.text: Blunt with comrade, one known for mangled Russian?

parts.note: Anthony Blunt, the art historian exposed as a Soviet spy
Guy Burgess, Blunt's fellow member of the Cambridge spy ring

explanation.surface: A blunt-speaking comrade is famous for murdering the Russian language.
explanation.walkthrough: Blunt is not an adjective but the spy's surname; his first name joins the surname of a fellow Cambridge spy.
explanation.definitionFit: The Clockwork Orange author invented Nadsat, a teenage slang built from distorted Russian words, so he is famous for warping that language.

clue.text: Perhaps Hughes cries out, describing shrew?

indicators.note: to describe a shape is to draw round it, so these letters go round another piece
out here means out of order, so the word before it is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
Kate is the shrew in Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew

explanation.surface: Ted Hughes, perhaps, shouts out a description of a nagging woman.
explanation.walkthrough: In a literary puzzle Hughes suggests the poet Ted, but the example is Sarah Hughes, the 2002 Olympic figure-skating champion.
explanation.definitionFit: Sarah Hughes won Olympic gold in women's figure skating, so she is one example of a sportswoman on the rink.

clue.text: Cassady returned carrying bit of dope, loaded

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the name is read right to left
one piece carrying another holds it inside itself

parts.note: Neal Cassady, the Beat hero who inspired Dean Moriarty in On the Road

indicators.note: only a bit of the word is used, its first letter

parts.note: the opening letter of dope

explanation.surface: The Beat writer Neal Cassady comes back from a trip carrying drugs, and is high.
explanation.walkthrough: Loaded is slang for drunk or high, which fits the Beat picture, but here it simply means burdened.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something carrying a heavy burden or cargo, as a ship or a cart is weighed down.

clue.text: Old priest backing Romeo in Mantua?

parts.note: ex- means former, so old

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the priest's name is read in reverse

parts.note: Eli, the priest who raised Samuel in the Bible

explanation.surface: An old friar supports Romeo when he is in Mantua.
explanation.walkthrough: The old priest sounds like Friar Laurence, who does help Romeo, but here it is the biblical Eli.
explanation.definitionFit: Romeo is banished from Verona and goes to Mantua, so there he is a person banished from his home city.

clue.text: Let in relative with hard and Causabon-like tone?

definitions.note: the clue gives a noun phrase; the answer is an adjective describing such a tone

indicators.note: in means the first piece goes inside the next one

parts.note: short for sister, a relative
to let is to permit
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A relative is allowed in, along with a hard man of dull, pasty complexion.
explanation.walkthrough: Casaubon is the dry old scholar in Eliot's Middlemarch, described with a pale, yellowish complexion.
explanation.definitionFit: The suffix makes a colour word meaning somewhat sickly yellow, which is the unhealthy skin tone of Eliot's ageing pedant.

clue.text: Literary books about caseless Wigan defendant?

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the first pieces go round the next

parts.note: lit is the short form of literary or literature

indicators.note: without its case the word loses its outer covering, its first and last letters

parts.note: Wigan with its two outer letters stripped
NT, the New Testament, a collection of books

explanation.surface: Literary works about a Lancashire town's legal defendant without a case to answer.
explanation.walkthrough: Caseless sounds legal, a defendant with no case against them, but it removes the outer letters of Wigan, a town in north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: A defendant is one party to a lawsuit, so the question mark marks it as an example of anyone involved in a court action.

clue.text: Fiftieth anniversary look at Fleming's estate

parts.note: a fiftieth anniversary is a golden one
to eye something is to look at it

explanation.surface: A visitor celebrates fifty years by gazing at Ian Fleming's house.
explanation.walkthrough: Fleming wrote the Bond novels at his Jamaican home, whose name he later gave to a Bond film title.
explanation.definitionFit: Ian Fleming's Jamaican estate on the north coast was named after a wartime operation and is where he wrote the Bond books.

clue.text: Mole at home around area on bank of adored river

indicators.note: around means one piece encircles another
the banks of a word are its two edges, its first and last letters

parts.note: the two edge letters of adored
R is the map abbreviation for river
someone at home is in
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A mole stays home near a riverbank that it loves.
explanation.walkthrough: The mole by the river suggests The Wind in the Willows, but it is Sue Townsend's diarist.
explanation.definitionFit: Adrian Mole is the teenage diarist in Sue Townsend's comic novels, so his surname stands in for his first name.

clue.text: This writer offers one way to get off smack

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a British novelist and journalist

definitions.text: one way to get off smack
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the willpower of one's own self, a means of quitting heroin, which is slang called smack

explanation.walkthrough: The novelist famously had a heroin habit, which makes the second meaning apt as well as punning; smack is slang for heroin.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of Great Apes and Umbrella is a writer, and his name read as two words describes quitting by sheer determination.

clue.text: Effete, upper-class outlaw upset by the French

parts.note: U is the standard abbreviation for upper-class

indicators.note: upset means turned over, so the word is reversed

parts.note: to outlaw something is to ban it
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A feeble aristocratic outlaw is beaten by the French.
explanation.definitionFit: Effete means feeble and lacking vigour, so someone effete is incapable of doing much.

clue.text: Noble, perhaps, to take care of old Italian poet

indicators.note: to take care of something is to hold it safe, so the first piece holds the next

parts.note: short for aristocrat, of whom a noble is an example
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A noble patron looks after an elderly Italian poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Renaissance poets did have noble patrons, so the surface is plausible; the noble supplies the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Ludovico Ariosto wrote Orlando Furioso, the sixteenth-century epic of chivalry, in Ferrara.

clue.text: Animal barking away that holds Carraclough's heart

indicators.note: one piece holds another inside it
barking away suggests going wild, so the word is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the heart of a word is the letter at its centre

parts.note: the central letter of the eleven in Carraclough

explanation.surface: A dog barks away while holding the heart of the boy who owns it.
explanation.walkthrough: Joe Carraclough is the boy in Lassie Come-Home, so barking suggests Lassie, but the creature is a crustacean.
explanation.definitionFit: This large crustacean of cold northern seas is a creature of the animal kingdom, a very general definition.

clue.text: A gulled gentleman lacks energy to be a composer

indicators.note: lacking something means doing without it, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: Roderigo is the foolish Venetian gentleman duped by Iago in Othello
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A deceived gentleman runs out of steam and ends up as a composer.
explanation.walkthrough: Gulled means fooled, which points to Shakespeare's dupe in Othello.
explanation.definitionFit: Joaquín Rodrigo was the Spanish composer of the Concierto de Aranjuez for guitar and orchestra.

clue.text: "The true art of — is the art of attention" (Samuel Johnson)

definitions.text: "The true art of — is the art of attention" (Samuel Johnson)

parts.words: "The true art of — is the art of attention"
parts.note: surface reading: a quotation from Johnson with a word missing
setter's reading: the missing word is the faculty of recall, which Johnson said depends on paying attention

explanation.walkthrough: The dash marks the gap; the answer is the word Johnson used in his essay in The Idler.
explanation.definitionFit: Johnson argued that recalling things well depends on attending to them closely in the first place, so the gap needs the faculty of recall.

clue.text: Buttercup, perhaps, by spring in old prison

parts.note: Buttercup is the heroine of The Princess Bride
a spring is a well, a source of water

explanation.surface: A buttercup grows by a spring next to the walls of an old prison.
explanation.walkthrough: Buttercup looks like a flower beside a spring, but it is the heroine of William Goldman's The Princess Bride.
explanation.definitionFit: Bridewell was a London house of correction, and its name became a general word for a gaol in Britain.

clue.text: Middle-Earth knight that's travelled by horse around and about?

indicators.note: about means turned about, facing back the other way
around means one piece goes round another

parts.note: to travel by horse is to ride, past tense
N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: A knight of Middle-earth rides around on horseback.
explanation.walkthrough: Tolkien's Elvish name for Middle-earth is this, and the knight on horseback fits his world.
explanation.definitionFit: In Tolkien's legendarium Endor is the Quenya Elvish word for the central continent, literally middle land.

clue.text: Note bit of dynamite that's going up and duck!

indicators.note: in a down entry going up means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: re is the second note of the sol-fa scale

indicators.note: only a bit of the word is used, its first letter

parts.note: the opening letter of dynamite
i.e. is the abbreviation for that is

explanation.surface: A warning: the dynamite is about to explode, so take cover!
explanation.walkthrough: Duck reads as the order to take cover, but it is the sea duck prized for its down.
explanation.definitionFit: The eider is a large northern sea duck whose soft breast feathers fill eiderdown quilts.

clue.text: Who wrote: "Blest is that government where no art thrives"?

definitions.text: Who wrote: "Blest is that government where no art thrives"?

parts.note: surface reading: a quiz question asking for the author of a quotation

parts.words: "Blest is that government where no art thrives"
parts.note: setter's reading: the line comes from the Elizabethan pamphleteer and satirist whose works were banned in 1599

explanation.walkthrough: A straight literary quiz question: the line is by Thomas Nashe, whose satires were burnt by order of the bishops in 1599.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Nashe was the Elizabethan satirist who wrote that ironic line praising states where artists cannot flourish.

clue.text: Without it, Gibson's 1988 work is just a great picture!

definitions.text: Without it, Gibson's 1988 work is just a great picture

parts.note: surface reading: a film or artwork by someone called Gibson, perhaps Mel
setter's reading: William Gibson's 1988 novel loses its last word and leaves the title of Leonardo's famous portrait

explanation.walkthrough: Gibson suggests Mel the film-maker, but it is William Gibson, whose 1988 cyberpunk novel's title starts with Leonardo's most famous portrait.
explanation.definitionFit: Remove the final word of Mona Lisa Overdrive and what remains is Mona Lisa, the great painting the clue mentions.

clue.text: My orders force Oceania's leader to change play

indicators.note: to change the letters is to put them in a different order

parts.note: all three words taken as written

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of Oceania

explanation.surface: A ruler of Orwell's Oceania orders a play to be rewritten.
explanation.walkthrough: Oceania's leader suggests Big Brother in Nineteen Eighty-Four, but it only gives one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Comedy of Errors is Shakespeare's farce of two sets of twins, one of his earliest stage plays.
